newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-RIVER PLATE BIDDING TO SCORE SHOCK WIN OVER JUVENTUS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RIVER PLATE BIDDING TO SCORE SHOCK WIN OVER JUVENTUS.

text.p: River Plate could be set to deliver yet another shock to Europeans who turn their noses up at the thought of South American club soccer when they meet Juventus in the Intercontinental Cup final in Tokyo on Tuesday..
South America has never managed to command the same respect on the club stage as it has at national team level.

Many outsiders find the foreign-influenced names bizarre -- Boca Juniors, The Strongest, Corinthians, Jorge Wilsterman, O'Higgins and Newell's Old Boys are but a few examples -- and the local competitions incomprehensible.

Meanwhile, the clubs are perpetually fighting a losing battle their top stars being exported to European and, more recently, Japanese clubs. Yet on the occasions that they meet their far richer European counterparts, South Americans come out on top more often than not.
Since the Intercontinental Cup, the unofficial world club championship, began in 1960, South America has taken the title 20 times against Europe's 13.
Surprisingly, South America have continued to have the upper hand in recent years despite the ever-widening financial gap between clubs from the two continents.

South American teams have won three of the last four finals, with even mightly Milan losing successive finals to Sao Paulo of Brazil and Velez Sarsfied of Argentina. They have also won on ten of the 16 occasions since the final became a one-match affair played in Tokyo. River Plate, who beat Romania's Steaua Bucharest on their only previous appearance in the match ten years ago, are in an excellent position to provide yet another "shock" result.

Nicknamed the "Millonaires", thanks to some spending sprees considered extravagent by local standards, River are currently top of the Argentine championship, having won ten of their 13 games and scored 34 goals.

Coached by former Argentine international Ramon Diaz, they have impressed not only with their statistics but also their attractive, attacking soccer, which may not fit in with the normal image of the Argentine game.
Like many South American clubs, River have an amazing ability to replenish talent as fast as they lose it and their team is brimming with promising young players.

These include striker 22-year-old striker Ariel Ortega, who already has several national team appearances to his credit, and 18-year-old Santiago Solari, who performed impressively in last Sunday's 4-0 win over San Lorenzo.

However, the team is masterminded by a veteran foreign player -- 35-year-old Uruguayan midfielder Enzo Francescoli who last year led his country to the Copa America title before announcing his international retirement.
Francescoli has been playing so well -- and Uruguay so badly -- that he was subsequently lured back to international soccer and has played in his country's last two games.
He limped off injured in the 1-0 defeat by Chile last week and missed the San Lorenzo game but is expected to be fit for Tuesday.
Chilean midfielder Marcelo Salas, who scored the winner against Uruguay, is another vital component of the team while marksman is Julio Cruz, topscorer in the Argentine championship with ten goals.
Argentina are the country to have won most Interncontinental titles, with seven to their credit, but Italy will draw level if the win on Tuesday.

Juventus, however, will do well to remember their previous encounter with South American opposition. They were beaten on penalties in the final of the pre-season Teresa Herrera tournament in Spain by the same Botafogo side that is currently discredited and languishing in 16th place in the Brazilian championship.

Juventus left London on Thursday night for Tokyo a day after their superb 1-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League and coach Marcello Lippi said his first challenge was to make sure the players overcome jet lag and the time difference.
Lippi wanted his players to sleep monm the plane and as soon as they arrived they trained rather than go to the hotel.
New Portuguese signing, defender Dimas, will be with the squad but is going along for the experience and will not play, Lippi said.
"This is a match that the players who helped us win the European Cup have earned. It's only right, and it's logical, that it belongs entirely to them," Lippi said.

For Juventus, winning the cup would be prestigious and be worth substantial bonuses to the players, but the main prizes for Juve this season are to retain the European Cup and win the Italian League with this trophy a distant third on the list of priorities.
